findings.headline: Council identifies £1.45m potential additional energy cost pressure in 2026/27 despite Q1 position on budget
findings.detail: Council's forecast remains sensitive to inflation and market pressures. Energy costs could create an additional £1.45m pressure in 2026/27, although Q1 has remained on budget. Future pay awards, workforce changes, collection rates, arrears, and bad-debt provisions are flagged as areas requiring close monitoring.
findings.matters: Energy costs are volatile and council-wide. If the £1.45m potential pressure materializes, it would erode approximately one-third of the current Q1 underspend and reinforce reliance on reserves or further service cuts.
findings.figures: £1.45m potential energy cost pressure
findings.quote: Energy costs could create an additional £1.45m pressure in 2026/27, although Q1 remains on budget.

findings.headline: Integration Joint Board forecasting £0.358m underspend but position described as 'finely balanced' with emerging risks
findings.detail: The IJB is forecasting a £0.358m full-year underspend at end of Q1. However, council describes the position as 'finely balanced and will require continued monitoring' with key risks relating to care demand, staffing, prescribing costs, savings delivery, and service redesign assumptions. Any movement in IJB position could impact the council's wider financial position.
findings.matters: The IJB covers social care and health integration. An apparently balanced position that council describes as 'finely balanced' with multiple directional risks (demand growth, staffing pressures, prescribing inflation) suggests future pressure is likely. IJB deficits have been common across Scottish local authorities.
findings.figures: £0.358m underspend
findings.quote: The overall position remains finely balanced and will require continued monitoring, with key risks relating to care demand, staffing, prescribing costs, savings delivery and the delivery of service redesign assumptions.

findings.headline: £4.870m favorable Q1 variance is explicitly attributed to temporary factors, not sustainable operational improvements
findings.detail: The council provides an explicit warning that the favorable £4.870m Q1 position 'should not be interpreted as evidence that the Council's underlying financial challenge has reduced.' Drivers include staffing vacancies where posts are held pending structural reviews, property income variances, and timing differences in expenditure. Council states variances 'may reverse or not recur in 2027/28.'
findings.matters: A lender reading a favorable Q1 position without this context would misjudge the council's underlying financial health. The explicit warning signals operational management is controlling spend short-term, but the structural deficit remains unresolved.
findings.figures: £4.870m under-budget, £1.865m Business Services vacancies
findings.quote: The favourable position should not be interpreted as evidence that the Council's underlying financial challenge has reduced... Members should therefore not assume that the full under-budget position is available to support future budget planning as some favourable variances may reverse or not recur in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Council deploying Risk and Inflation Reserve for £4.458m investment in maintenance, roads, and emergency costs
findings.detail: Council has approved drawdown of £4.458m from the Risk and Inflation Reserve to address 'priority resilience, infrastructure and asset-related pressures' including repairs/maintenance (£1.408m), roads (£1.000m), learning estate safety (£0.200m), winter maintenance (£0.600m), emergency incident costs (£1.000m), and uninsured losses (£0.250m). The Reserve balance is forecast at £13.598m at 31 March 2027. Council cautions that reserves are finite and deployment 'does not remove the need to identify and deliver recurring savings.'
findings.matters: Use of reserves to fund operational pressures and capital maintenance signals that recurring revenues are insufficient to cover approved services and essential infrastructure. Reserves are being deployed as a buffer for current pressures, not held as contingency.
findings.figures: £4.458m investment, £13.598m forecast balance, £0.323m RSG transfer, £111,556 LACER transfer
findings.quote: Council previously approved investment of £4.458m from the Risk and Inflation Reserve to address priority resilience, infrastructure and asset-related pressures... reserves are a finite resource and can only provide temporary support.

findings.headline: £1.700m (18%) of 2026/27 savings remain classified as Amber with delivery still subject to management action
findings.detail: While 82% of savings (£7.554m) are complete or on track, £1.700m remain unconfirmed. Within this, £1.100m is expected to be delivered but awaits confirmation. Most critically, £0.450m (in Education and Children's Services) is subject to 'enhanced monitoring and confirmation of sustainable underspends,' suggesting some savings may not recur or may require intervention.
findings.matters: Amber-rated savings requiring enhanced monitoring may not deliver as planned, creating additional in-year pressure on the council's budget and increasing reliance on reserves or further service cuts.
findings.figures: £1.700m (18%) Amber, £1.100m expected, £0.450m enhanced monitoring
findings.quote: £1.700m (18%) assessed as Amber... £0.450m is subject to enhanced monitoring and confirmation of sustainable underspends.

findings.headline: Nine of eleven strategic budget risks remain rated High despite budget approval in February 2026
findings.detail: The Strategic Risk Register shows nine of eleven risks identified at budget-setting remain High after existing controls. These span five themes: financial sustainability (structural budget gap and reliance on non-recurring funding), economic volatility (inflation and pay pressures), capital and asset resilience (IT investment constraints and aging infrastructure), demand and service pressures (IJB funding, demographic change), and financial exposure (uninsured claims).
findings.matters: Persistence of high risks despite budget controls suggests underlying vulnerabilities are not being resolved. Multiple directional risks (inflation, demand, pay pressures) indicate future deterioration is likely rather than improvement.
findings.figures: 9 of 11 strategic risks rated High
findings.quote: Of the 11 strategic risks reported in February 2026 when the budget was approved, nine remain High after existing controls, requiring continued senior management and Member oversight.

findings.headline: Only 9% of 2026/27 capital budget spent by end of Q1; Peterhead projects reprofiled to 2027/28
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure to 30 June 2026 was £10.289m against a £113.633m budget (9% spend). The General Services Capital Plan forecasts a £8.008m underspend. The Peterhead Community Campus and Cultural Quarter projects are being reprofiled from 2026/27 into 2027/28, reflecting revised delivery timescales as projects move from development to construction. Some grant-funded budgets are time-limited and must be spent by 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Very low early-year capital spend creates delivery risk for the full-year budget and compliance risk for time-limited grants. Reprofiling of major levelling-up projects may affect grant conditions and create future cash flow pressures.
findings.figures: £10.289m (9%) spent, £113.633m budget, £8.008m underspend, £1.311m Tier 1 Bus Infrastructure, £0.540m Active Travel Tier 2
findings.quote: Actual expenditure to 30 June 2026 was £10.289m (9%)... The Quarter 1 variance reflects revised delivery timescales, with expenditure now expected to be incurred over later financial years, mainly 2027/28.

findings.headline: Council's medium-term structural gap reaches £158.4m by 2030/31 despite forecast underspend of £4.870m in Q1
findings.detail: The General Fund is forecasting an underspend of £4.870m at Q1, but council guidance explicitly cautions that this favorable in-year position masks persistent structural challenges. Even after accounting for carry-forward funding and bad debt reviews, the potential gap in 2027/28 is £38.9m, rising to £158.4m by 2030/31. The Q1 underspend is driven by temporary factors (staffing vacancies, timing differences) rather than sustainable improvements.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether short-term performance improvements address underlying insolvency risks. A £158.4m gap over four years indicates the council cannot fund approved services on recurring revenues alone.
findings.figures: £4.870m underspend Q1, £38.9m potential gap 2027/28, £158.4m by 2030/31
findings.quote: the structural gap still reaches £158.4m by 2030/31, demonstrating that the Council's medium-term financial challenge remains substantial despite the favourable Quarter 1 position

findings.detail: The capital budget fell from £113.6m (June 2026) to £101.6m (September 2026). findings.headline: Free school meals uptake among entitled secondary pupils dropped from 63% to 47%, creating policy delivery uncertainty
findings.detail: Uptake of free school meals by eligible secondary pupils (S1-S6) fell sharply from 63% in 2024/25 to 47% in 2025/26, reversing the prior year's spike. The council attributes this to it being 'broadly in line with previous years' (46% in 2023/24), but does not explain the cause of the 63% peak or the subsequent drop. The council's target is 50%.
findings.matters: This volatility in a statutory service that represents both a policy commitment and a cost line is unexplained. The sharp movements year-on-year suggest either policy changes, school-level implementation variations, or genuine demand shifts that lack clear management explanation.
findings.quote: Free school meal uptake among entitled secondary school pupils (S1–S6) was 47% in 2025/26, compared with 63% in 2024/25 and 46% in 2023/24

findings.headline: Procurement activity delivered £1.3m of actual savings during the year
findings.detail: The Finance and Governance Directorate achieved £1.3m in savings through procurement activity. Procurement process improvements and strengthened guidance also enhanced compliance and consistency across the council.
findings.matters: Delivery of procurement savings in-year demonstrates effective spend management and cost control discipline at a point when councils face inflationary pressures.
findings.figures: £1.3 million savings delivered
findings.quote: Procurement activity has delivered £1.3 million of savings during the year, while improvements to procurement processes and guidance have strengthened compliance and consistency

findings.headline: Sheltered housing review identified £15m capital and £1m annual revenue savings across 56 schemes
findings.detail: A comprehensive review of all 56 sheltered housing schemes following place standard assessments and consultation with over 600 tenants identified substantial long-term savings through service reshaping. The report does not specify whether these savings are being delivered in 2025/26 or are committed for future implementation.
findings.matters: Identified property and service savings of this scale demonstrate active asset management and potential material improvement to long-term financial sustainability. However, the timing and certainty of delivery is material to current financial risk assessment.
findings.figures: £15m capital savings over 10 years; £1m per annum revenue savings identified
findings.quote: The review will provide £15m in capital savings over the next 10 years, and £1m per year in revenue savings

findings.headline: Health and social care partnership operating under sustained financial constraint with rising demand complexity
findings.detail: The Integration Joint Board reported the partnership operating in a highly challenging environment throughout 2025/26 with sustained demand pressures, increasing complexity of need, and significant financial constraints. In response, a Medium-Term Financial Strategy was developed and a balanced revenue budget agreed for 2026/27. The partnership remains focused on delivering best value and reshaping services within available resources.
findings.matters: Health and social care is typically the largest or second-largest budget item for a council. Rising demand and complexity alongside financial constraint signals risk of service rationing, cost control challenges, or reserve drawdown. The forward planning suggests anticipated future pressure.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the document
findings.quote: The Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership continued to operate in a highly challenging environment during 2025/26, with sustained demand pressures, increasing complexity of need and significant financial constraints across the health and social care system

findings.headline: Public confidence that the council takes account of resident views has fallen sharply to 28%, down from 41% a year earlier
findings.detail: The proportion of residents agreeing the council takes their views into account dropped to 28% in 2025/26, from 41% in 2024/25 and 47% in 2023/24. The council's target is 74%. The report acknowledges this disconnect explicitly: despite significant service investment and improvements, these gains are not being reflected in public perception.
findings.matters: Declining public confidence in council governance and engagement is a creditworthiness indicator. A persistent gap between delivery and perception suggests either communication failure or genuine governance challenges, both of which affect stakeholder confidence.
findings.quote: despite significant investment, activity and engagement, these improvements are not always reflected in public perception measures. This reinforces the importance of continuing to work closely with communities, ensuring feedback informs decision-making and strengthening understanding

findings.detail: While the council reports no direct financial or staffing implications at the current stage, it explicitly acknowledges that going forward, Programme for Government outcomes may materially affect future revenue, capital, staffing and governance requirements. These impacts will need to be assessed as consultations progress and outcomes become clearer.
findings.matters: Signals the council expects potentially material changes to revenue and governance requirements in the medium term, indicating planning uncertainty relevant to lenders and finance directors assessing multi-year sustainability

findings.paper_title: Programme for Government 2026–2031 and Public Service Reform
findings.headline: Scottish Government proposes replacing 14 territorial Health Boards with two Strategic Health Boards, creating major implications for NHS Grampian and Aberdeenshire
findings.detail: The Programme for Government signals one of its most significant structural changes: consolidating 14 territorial Health Boards into two Strategic Health Boards. Aberdeenshire Council acknowledges this could have major implications for NHS Grampian, the Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership, workforce planning, service commissioning and accountability arrangements. The full local impact is not yet clear and will be subject to Scottish Government consultation.
findings.matters: Governance restructuring affecting health and social care delivery directly impacts council service integration, commissioning arrangements, workforce requirements and potentially revenue and capital needs in the medium term
findings.figures: 14 territorial Health Boards consolidated to 2 Strategic Health Boards
findings.quote: One of the most significant proposals in the 2026 PfG is replacing 14 territorial Health Boards with two Strategic Health Boards. This could have major implications for NHS Grampian, Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership, workforce planning, service commissioning and accountability arrangements.

findings.headline: Bad debt provisions increased by £1.55m to £39.72m in 2026/27, with Council Tax bad debt provision rising £1.00m despite stated strong collection rates
findings.detail: Total provisions are forecast to rise by £1.55m to £39.72m. Council Tax bad debt provision increases by £1.00m (to £20.76m) and other bad debt by £0.55m (to £6.84m). While the council states that 'Collection rates remain strong,' the increase in provisions reflects expectations of higher write-off or uncollectible sums. This may signal either prudent management or early signs of collection deterioration among residents.
findings.matters: Rising bad debt provisions are a leading indicator of potential income risk, even when current collection rates appear stable. An increase of £1.00m in Council Tax provisions suggests management's assessment of future collectibility has deteriorated.
findings.figures: Total provisions £39.72m (increase £1.55m); Council Tax bad debt £20.76m (increase £1.00m); Other bad debt £6.84m (increase £0.55m)
findings.quote: Forecast provisions rise by £1.55m to £39.72m in 2026/27 in line with budget approval.

findings.headline: Energy and market volatility sensitivity analysis indicates potential additional cost pressure of £1.45m for 2026/27, currently excluded from forecast and flagged for Q2 review
findings.detail: The council has conducted sensitivity analysis identifying a potential downside risk of approximately £1.45m in energy costs for 2026/27 (General Fund £1.184m, HRA £0.200m, IJB £0.067m). This is explicitly excluded from the Q1 forecast and noted as requiring review at Q2. Energy is flagged as 'the key downside risk' and the council notes that 'energy, fuel, transport, commissioned services and supplier workforce costs should remain under close review.'
findings.matters: A £1.45m downside sensitivity represents 30% of the Q1 favourable variance. If realised, it would reverse the current positive position and require further remedial action. Energy volatility in the current environment makes this a material tail risk.
findings.figures: £1.45m potential energy cost pressure (not in forecast): General Fund £1.184m, HRA £0.200m, IJB £0.067m; could exceed Q1 favourable variance of £4.870m if combined with other pressures
findings.quote: As reported in June, estimates indicate a potential additional cost pressure of c.£1.45m in 2026/27 (General Fund £1.184m, HRA £0.200m and IJB £0.067m) for energy costs. This estimate is a sensitivity scenario and not included in the Q1 forecast position but will be revisited and updated at Q2.

findings.headline: 11 council-wide strategic risks remain at Critical or High severity after mitigation, with 9 scoring Critical (20–25) before controls
findings.detail: The council maintains 11 council-wide strategic risks at SLT level. Before mitigation controls, 9 score Critical on the 5×5 matrix: Structural budget gap (25), Non-recurring funding (20), Inflationary shock (20), Uninsured claims exposure (20), Capital affordability (20), IJB funding (20), IT capital funding (20), Prioritisation & demographics (20), and Ageing infrastructure (20). After mitigation, 9 remain High or Critical, indicating that existing controls do not eliminate material risks.
findings.matters: A large number of persistent Critical risks after mitigation indicates either that control measures are insufficient, or that the risks are structural and difficult to manage. The concentration of 20-point risks suggests multiple concurrent shocks could materially worsen the position.
findings.figures: 11 total council-wide risks; 9 Critical before controls (20–25); 9 High/Critical after mitigation; Structural gap risk 25/16; Non-recurring funding 20/12; Inflationary shock 20/16; Capital affordability 20/16
findings.quote: 11 council-wide risks sit at Strategic Leadership Team level; 9 score Critical before controls and 9 remain High after mitigation.

findings.headline: General Services capital plan only 9.1% spent by June with £8.01m forecast variance; HRA capital at 5.6% with £7.32m variance attributed to timing
findings.detail: Capital spending is significantly slower than budgeted. General Services (revised budget £113.63m) has spent only £10.29m by end-June, forecast to total £105.63m (£8.01m below budget). HRA capital (revised budget £31.11m) has spent only £1.75m by June, forecast £23.79m (£7.32m below budget). Main delays are Peterhead Cultural Quarter, flooding works, CRD Digital reprofiling, and Housing Improvement Plan (HIP2). Timing is cited as the reason, but large underspends in Q1 on capital programmes could indicate deferral rather than simple timing.
findings.matters: Capital underspend can mask deferral of necessary work driven by affordability constraints rather than genuine timing differences. If capital spending is being deferred to manage the structural deficit, this defers maintenance and improvement liabilities into future years.
findings.figures: General Services: £113.63m budget, £10.29m spent (9.1%), £105.63m forecast (£8.01m variance). HRA: £31.11m budget, £1.75m spent (5.6%), £23.79m forecast (£7.32m variance). HIP2 variance £7.25m.
findings.quote: Main variance reasons: Education & Children (£5.49m) and Environment & Infrastructure (£2.51m), driven by Peterhead Cultural Quarter, flooding works and CRD Digital reprofiling.

findings.headline: Integration Joint Board Adult Services Community Care is £2.106m over budget, driven by third-party care packages, complex needs and high-cost transitions
findings.detail: Within the IJB, Council Social Care overall shows £1.363m adverse variance. The largest pressure is Adult Services Community Care at £2.106m over budget, driven by demand and complexity factors: third-party care packages, complex needs, and high-cost transitions. This overspend persists despite substantial offsets (AHP £1.015m, Hosted Services £0.618m, Primary Care £0.387m underspends). The council flags activity and care-package assumptions as at risk and subject to demand volatility.
findings.matters: Social care represents one of the least controllable local authority cost areas. A £2.106m overspend signals demand and complexity trends that could worsen through the MTFS period and are difficult to reverse through conventional savings.
findings.figures: Adult Services Community Care £2.106m over; Council Social Care overall £1.363m adverse; IJB total £0.358m favourable (due to NHSG offsets)
findings.quote: Adult Services – Community Care is £2.106m over budget, driven by third-party care packages, complex needs and high-cost transitions.

findings.headline: £1.700m (18% of total) of budgeted £9.254m savings are at amber risk, including £1.550m Education target dependent on removing sustainable underspends
findings.detail: Savings delivery shows £7.554m on track or complete (green/complete status) but £1.700m classified as amber (partially delivered or off track but recoverable). The largest amber item is Education & Children's Services (£1.550m), which is described as being delivered through 'removal of sustainable underspends'—euphemism for cutting into service delivery. Housing and Building Standards saving (£0.150m) is dependent on ICT system implementation.
findings.matters: Savings are the primary mechanism for bridging the structural deficit. Amber items that do not materialise will widen the gap further. The Education description suggests the council may be relying on assumptions that underspends are truly sustainable.
findings.figures: £9.254m total budgeted savings; £7.554m complete/on track; £1.700m amber; Education £1.550m; Housing/Building Standards £0.150m
findings.quote: Education and Children's Services (£1.550m): savings target to be delivered through enhanced in-year financial monitoring and removal of sustainable underspends; continued monitoring is required to confirm delivery.

findings.headline: Cumulative funding gap of £158.4m by 2030/31 requires recurring savings, transformation and disinvestment to close
findings.detail: The council projects a funding gap that grows from £0m (2026/27) to £38.9m (2027/28), £69.6m (2028/29), £116.8m (2029/30), and £158.4m (2030/31). This structural gap is the council's dominant financial sustainability risk and requires action beyond one-time solutions or capital deferrals. The gap reflects a structural mismatch between recurring spending and recurring income.
findings.matters: A £158m structural gap over four years represents material financial stress. A lender must assess whether the council has credible plans to deliver this level of recurring savings without compromising service viability.
findings.quote: The structural gap still reaches £158.4m by 2030/31, requiring recurring savings, transformation and disinvestment.

findings.headline: Q1 favourable variance of £4.870m and 2027/28 gap improvement of £3.5m are driven by non-recurring items, not structural improvement
findings.detail: The council's short-term positive performance is largely attributable to reduced capital financing requirements (£2.911m) from lower 2025/26 borrowing, business services underspends, and the 2027/28 gap improvement coming from EPR carry-forward funding (one-off) and bad-debt reviews. Management explicitly states that 'Favourable short-term signals are largely non-recurring' and notes work has only just begun on 2027/28+ recurring options and prioritisation.
findings.matters: A lender must distinguish between sustainable improvement and one-time gains. Relying on non-recurring funding to bridge deficits is a warning sign of underlying structural stress.
findings.figures: £4.870m Q1 favourable variance; 2027/28 cumulative gap £38.9m (improved by £3.5m from February); £3.580m EPR funding carried forward; Capital Financing variance £2.911m
findings.quote: Favourable short-term signals are largely non-recurring; work has started on 2027/28+ options, recurring savings and prioritisation.

findings.matters: Major regeneration projects commonly slip; Levelling Up funding is time-limited and non-fungible. If this project does not meet the delivery timetable, funding is lost and the council cannot reallocate it—adding urgency and execution risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5B - General Services Capital Plan 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Total capital expenditure falls 57% from £115.249m in 2027/28 to £49.269m in 2028/29, and continues declining to £36.152m by 2030/31.
findings.detail: The capital plan shows a sharp step change in ambition. After 2027/28, the council's capital spending baseline is significantly lower, declining further each year. This pattern reflects the ending of one-off grant-funded projects (Levelling Up, education expansions) that drive the 2027/28 peak.
findings.matters: A sharp reduction in capital spending can indicate either prudent management of declining grant income or deferred asset maintenance backlog. A lender needs to understand whether the baseline capital programme is sufficient for the council's assets and service continuity.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5B - General Services Capital Plan 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Six Scottish Government grants and Levelling Up funding totalling £14.269m end after 2026/27, and Levelling Up support halves then ends by 2028/29.
findings.detail: Grants ending in 2026/27 include 1140 Hours (£2.310m), Free School Meals Expansion (£510k), Road Safety Fund (£920k), Bairns' Hoose (£192k), and Tier 2 Active Travel (£540k). Levelling Up funding falls from £8.315m (2026/27) to £4.916m (2027/28) to zero. These funds enable the 2027/28 peak; once they end, capital expenditure drops to £49.269m—a 57% reduction.
findings.matters: Time-limited grants create cliff edges in funding. When they end, councils must either cut projects or find alternative financing. This plan shows capital expenditure dropping sharply after 2028/29, signalling that the peaks are unsustainable without grant funding.

findings.matters: Large concentrations of capital spending in a single year indicate delivery risk; schools projects often slip, and a lender needs confidence that the timetable is realistic and the consequences of re-profiling are understood.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5B - General Services Capital Plan 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Aberdeenshire plans to increase prudential borrowing by £20.166m (34%) in 2027/28 to £79.846m, the highest point in the plan.
findings.detail: The financing table shows borrowing increasing from £59.680m in 2026/27 to £79.846m in 2027/28, then declining sharply to £21.761m in 2028/29. This concentrated peak is driven by the timing of capital projects, particularly education spending, which concentrates in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A 34% increase in borrowing in a single year is a significant refinancing and liquidity event; a lender needs to understand whether this is within the council's prudential borrowing limits and whether it is sustainable given the sharp decline thereafter.

findings.headline: Landscape Services (£500k) is subject to a 'significant change' in delivery model relying on community groups to replace council staff.
findings.detail: The council describes this as 'a significant change to the current level of service delivered by the Landscape Team'. Mitigation relies on 'increased involvement of community groups, supported through engagement, dialogue and capacity‑building activity', essentially transferring service delivery from council employees to volunteers.
findings.matters: Service delivery is being transferred to external parties (community groups) outside the council's direct control; if community capacity does not materialise or uptake is lower than planned, service gaps emerge.

findings.quote: This proposal represents a significant change to the current level of service delivered by the Landscape Team. Mitigation will focus on increased involvement of community groups, supported through engagement, dialogue and capacity‑building activity.

findings.headline: Sheltered housing support service (£357k) has been removed following deregistration of care facilities.
findings.detail: A service described as mandatory under Care Commission requirements has been ceased. The council states deregistration 'has taken place' (past tense) as part of a broader reshaping of sheltered housing. The item is marked complete, meaning this cut has already been implemented.
findings.matters: The council has removed a mandated support service for vulnerable residents; this signals both a change to the council's care delivery role and completion of a significant service closure.
findings.figures: £357,000 complete
findings.quote: This has been a mandatory service in line with Care Commission requirements, but will no longer be required following deregistration, which has taken place as part of the review to reshape Sheltered Housing.

findings.headline: The Capital From Current Revenue estimate for roads has jumped from £2.5m to £3.5m, and the council is using £1m of this upward revision to fund 2026/27 revenue savings.
findings.detail: The council initially estimated road maintenance spending eligible for CFCR treatment at £2.5m. 'Following further detailed analysis of qualifying Roads Maintenance expenditure, this estimate has been revised to £3.5m.' The council is capturing £1m of this upward revision as a revenue saving, either reflecting previous underestimation or a change in what qualifies as capital.
findings.matters: Capital classification is regulatory and could change; if the £3.5m estimate reverses or regulatory treatment shifts, the council loses a £1m funding source for core services.
findings.figures: £2.5 million revised to £3.5 million; £1,000,000 captured as 2026/27 saving
findings.quote: It was initially anticipated that expenditure eligible to be reclassified as capital through Capital From Current Revenue (CFCR) in 2026/27 would be around £2.5 million. However, following further detailed analysis of qualifying Roads Maintenance expenditure, this estimate has been revised to £3.5 million.

findings.headline: A new charging policy for disabled home adaptations affecting vulnerable groups is marked amber delivery status.
findings.detail: The council proposes introducing charges for minor adaptations (grab rails, handrails, lowered thresholds) previously provided free. The saving is £150k. The item is marked amber and the paper acknowledges it requires 'Intended mitigation measures, alternative options, and opportunities to minimise harm or disadvantage' for vulnerable groups including older adults, disabled people, and those on low incomes.
findings.matters: The policy is not yet locked in (amber status); implementation risk is high given consultation requirements and the need to assess impact on vulnerable groups.
findings.figures: £150,000 amber status
findings.quote: The proposed introduces a financial charge for the provision and installation of these minor adaptations

findings.headline: Two staffing services totalling £330,000 in savings depend on vacancy trends continuing, with explicit acknowledgment of financial risk if trends reverse.
findings.detail: Community Learning and Development staffing (£220k) and Instrumental Music staffing (£110k) both assume current vacancy management patterns persist. The council explicitly states in both cases that 'if historic staffing trends do not continue, additional disinvestment measures may be required to manage the resulting budget pressure.' Both are marked green despite this risk disclosure.
findings.matters: If staffing vacancy trends change—which is a hiring/labour market decision outside council control—£330k in assumed savings will not materialise and the council will need emergency cuts.
findings.figures: £220,000 + £110,000 = £330,000; green status despite risk
findings.quote: However, this approach carries a financial risk, and if historic staffing trends do not continue, additional disinvestment measures may be required to manage the resulting budget pressure.

findings.headline: The largest single savings item at £1.55m has amber delivery status, creating risk to the council's budget plan.
findings.detail: The 'In-Year Financial Oversight and Resource Realignment' item is marked amber and depends on enhanced monitoring to identify 'sustainable underspends' through vacancy management, spending controls, and procurement efficiencies. This is by far the largest single item in the 2026/27 savings plan; if it slips or fails, the council faces material budget pressure.
findings.matters: The largest component of the council's budget-balancing plan is flagged as at-risk; failure to deliver would open a deficit.
findings.figures: £1,550,300 amber status
findings.quote: Enhanced in‑year financial monitoring will identify and remove sustainable underspends arising from vacancy management, essential‑only spending controls, and procurement efficiencies.

findings.headline: Five new funding allocations totalling £0.607m are awaiting service confirmation of need before the council commits to spending them.
findings.detail: School Meals (£0.097m), Discretionary Housing Payment additional (£0.222m), Scottish Recommended Allowance uplift (£0.236m), Nature Restoration (£0.041m), and WFWF correction (£0.011m) are marked as new or additional funding, but with status 'Confirm Service need budget'. Services have not yet confirmed whether they will actually require these allocations.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed demand for £0.607m of funded allocations means the council cannot yet forecast whether spending will match available funds in-year, affecting reserve outturn predictions.
findings.figures: School Meals £0.097m, DHP £0.222m, SRA uplift £0.236m, Nature Restoration £0.041m, WFWF £0.011m
findings.quote: New/additional funding – service to confirm if they need budget

findings.headline: Two funded services are receiving less than Aberdeenshire budgeted for them, with the council drawing £0.023m from reserves to maintain spending levels.
findings.detail: Real Living Wage uplift was redetermined at £0.869m versus the council's budget assumption of £0.872m, a shortfall of £0.003m. Scottish Disability Payments was redetermined at £0.089m versus the budget assumption of £0.109m, a shortfall of £0.020m. The council's response is to cover both shortfalls from reserves rather than reduce service provision.
findings.matters: Drawing reserves to cover shortfalls in services the council assumed were fully funded signals forecasting errors and ongoing budget pressure in core service areas.
findings.figures: Real Living Wage shortfall £0.003m; Disability Payments shortfall £0.020m; total reserve draw £0.023m
findings.quote: Note minor difference in assumption, fund from Reserve

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing requirement reduced by £7.98m as capital expenditure forecast falls.
findings.detail: The council forecast prudential borrowing of £12.76m against an approved budget of £20.74m. This £7.98m reduction is a direct consequence of lower capital expenditure driven by HIP programme delays. Reduced borrowing is positive for debt levels, though it reflects deferred spending rather than cost control.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor planned debt take-on. Understanding that this reduction is driven by programme delays, not affordability gains, is essential for assessing execution risk and debt trajectory.
findings.figures: Approved prudential borrowing £20,739k, forecast £12,760k, variance £7,979k under budget
findings.quote: Prudential Borrowing 20,739 1,196 12,760 7,979

findings.headline: Housing Improvement Plan is forecast to deliver only £3.05m of its £10.3m budget due to delays in HIP2 commencement.
findings.detail: The council's flagship housing capital programme is significantly underspent. The HIP budget of £10.3m is now forecast to deliver only £3.05m, creating a £7.25m shortfall with expenditure reprofiled into future financial years. This single programme accounts for 99% of the total £7.3m HRA capital variance.
findings.matters: Project delivery delays on the largest HRA capital programme raise questions about execution capacity and signal broader capital delivery risk. Housing stock improvements planned for this year are deferred.
findings.figures: HIP approved budget £10,300k, forecast £3,050k, variance £7,250k; total HRA capital approved £31,110k, forecast £23,792k
findings.quote: The forecast underspend is primarily due to delays in the commencement of the HIP2 project, resulting in a reduced level of activity during 2026/27 and the reprofiling of expenditure into future financial years.

findings.headline: City Region Deal digital programme delayed; deadline extended to 31 December 2027.
findings.detail: The CRD Digital Challenge Fund is behind schedule with only 5 of 10 projects signed off and 5 more progressing. Scottish Government has agreed a deadline extension. £587k of the £1,036k budget is now forecast to fall into 2027/28.
findings.matters: Recurring project delays on strategic partnerships signal delivery risk and questions about the council's capacity to execute capital programmes.
findings.figures: £587k variance on revised budget of £1,036k
findings.quote: The Digital Challenge Fund has encountered delays in getting underway with 5 projects signed off and a further 5 progressing. An extension to 31 Dec 2027 has been agreed with Scottish Government

findings.headline: Scottish Government flooding grant cannot be spent in time; will require borrowing to replace it in future years.
findings.detail: General Capital Grant for flooding works cannot be deployed within 2026/27 as the council cannot scope and procure delivery in a single year. Since the grant cannot be carried forward, the council will substitute prudential borrowing in later years to complete the programme. This converts concessional grant funding into debt.
findings.matters: The council is unable to access free funding on time and will incur interest costs to replace it, materially worsening its financial position.
findings.figures: £1,870k variance on flooding; GCG cannot be carried forward
findings.quote: GCG cannot be carried forward and will require grant funding to be swapped for borrowing in later years.

findings.headline: Peterhead Cultural Quarter re-profiled by £5.5m to 2027/28 with unquantified building strip-out costs.
findings.detail: The £13.8m Levelling Up Funded project is being pushed from 2026/27 to 2027/28 to align with post-contract cashflow. The council has not quantified risks from initial building strip-out. The paper notes the extent of resulting works and costs remains unknown, creating budget uncertainty.
findings.matters: A major externally-funded project with undefined cost exposure in its early phase affects confidence in project control and true capital commitments.
findings.figures: £5,494k variance on revised budget of £13,809k
findings.quote: A risk allocation for potential issues arising from the initial building strip-out has not yet been included, as the extent of any resulting works and associated costs remains unknown.

findings.headline: Council must realign resources to priorities and demographics; pace of financial recovery depends on timely reallocation
findings.detail: The council states that financial recovery depends on timely decisions to redirect limited revenue, workforce and capital capacity from legacy spending patterns to areas of greatest strategic importance and demographic pressure. Work is continuing through budget planning, transformation and service reviews to identify where disinvestment or redesign is required. Progress is framed as a critical dependency for recovery.
findings.matters: Resource misalignment indicates spending may not match statutory need or strategic priorities, risking persistent overspends and ineffective resource use. Lenders need evidence that the council can make difficult disinvestment decisions at pace rather than spreading resources thinly across legacy activities.
findings.figures: Resource prioritization (STR-10) scored 4×5 = 20; work continuing through budget planning, transformation and service reviews; pace of recovery explicitly dependent on these decisions
findings.quote: The pace of financial recovery depends on timely decisions to redirect limited revenue, workforce and capital capacity to the areas of greatest impact.

findings.headline: Energy and broader inflation volatility increased following July 2026 Ofgem price cap rise; cumulative medium-term risk
findings.detail: The external environment deteriorated following increases in wholesale gas prices and the July 2026 increase in the Ofgem energy price cap. While the council's 2026/27 budget assumptions appear broadly prudent at present, the risk is cumulative: if inflation in energy, fuel, transport, commissioned services and capital costs exceed current assumptions over the medium term, this will widen the structural budget gap and pressure reserves.
findings.matters: Inflation hits councils across multiple budget lines simultaneously. If it exceeds assumptions significantly, it accelerates both the structural gap and reserve depletion. The council is already managing capital inflation by cutting scope; revenue inflation could force service cuts.
findings.figures: Inflationary shock (STR-03) scored 4×5 = 20; external environment deteriorated; cumulative pressure on MTFS if assumptions exceeded
findings.quote: The external environment has deteriorated in relation to energy and wider inflation volatility, particularly following increases in wholesale gas prices and the July 2026 increase in the Ofgem price cap. These developments reinforce the need to continue monitoring energy, fuel, transport, commissioned services, income collection, and capital affordability risks through Q1/Q2 reporting.

findings.headline: Capital plan affordability eroding; services responding by cutting scope rather than delivering investment
findings.detail: Rising construction inflation, supply-chain pressures, increased borrowing costs and reduced capital receipts and grants threaten the capital plan. Global geopolitical instability has increased volatility in fuel, energy, materials and transport. Rather than find additional funding, services are managing entirely through delivery trade-offs: reducing scope and specification, delivering fewer outputs, and reprofiling works to later years. This defers capital maintenance and asset replacement.
findings.matters: Repeated capital underperformance indicates the council cannot deliver its strategic investment programme. Deferred maintenance and asset replacement eventually force emergency spending or service failure. Rising borrowing costs may also force the council to borrow more than planned to maintain capital activity.
findings.figures: Capital affordability (STR-05) scored 4×5 = 20; services managing inflation 'almost entirely through delivery trade-offs'
findings.quote: In the absence of additional funding capacity, services are managing inflation almost entirely through delivery trade-offs - reducing scope/ specification, delivering fewer outputs, reprofiling works to later years, and reprioritising activity within rolling programmes.

findings.headline: Integration Joint Board Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecasts substantial deficit by 2030/31
findings.detail: The Integration Joint Board, which delivers health and social care services delegated to the council, has reported a better-than-expected 2025/26 position with lower drawdown from council reserves than budgeted. However, its Medium-Term Financial Strategy forecasts a significant deficit by 2030/31. This will create a recurrent funding gap that the council and NHS partner will need to address through additional contributions or rapid service redesign.
findings.matters: The IJB deficit represents a material claim on the council's finances over the next four years. It will either require the council to find additional funding for health and social care or force it to reduce investment in other statutory services. This directly affects the council's ability to manage its broader budget.
findings.figures: IJB's MTFS forecasting deficit of £66.180m by 2030/31; incorporated into council's MTFS projections; 2025/26 reserve draw lower than anticipated
findings.quote: The IJB's MTFS is forecasting a deficit of £66.180m but 2030/31 which has been factored into the Council's MTFS projections.

findings.headline: Council using reserves and one-off savings to balance budget rather than delivering recurrent solutions
findings.detail: The council is relying on reserves, one-off savings, temporary grants, fiscal flexibilities and vacancy management to balance the annual budget. These sources do not address underlying structural pressures. The council explicitly states there remains a need to deliver recurring savings. This approach reduces reserves, limits financial resilience and increases the risk of inability to meet statutory duties.
findings.matters: One-off measures indicate the budget is not genuinely balanced; they create a future shortfall. Lenders must understand the rate at which reserves are being consumed and when permanent fixes will arrive, as exhausted reserves force immediate service cuts or borrowing.
findings.figures: Non-recurring funding risk (STR-02) scored 4×5 = 20; Q1 2026/27 under-budget also attributed to non-recurring factors
findings.quote: These are one-off in nature and there remains a need to deliver recurring savings.

findings.headline: Structural budget gap remains unresolved; 2025/26 improvement attributed to non-recurring factors
findings.detail: The council's apparent improved 2025/26 outturn and Q1 2026/27 favorable position are both driven by non-recurring factors, not sustainable improvement. The underlying structural gap—where recurring expenditure exceeds sustainable recurring funding—persists. The council acknowledges this may grow over the medium term due to increasing demand, inflation, pay awards, legislative requirements and constrained government funding.
findings.matters: A persistent structural gap signals the council cannot sustain its current service delivery from recurring revenue and will face ongoing deficits unless it delivers recurrent savings at scale. Lenders need confidence in the credibility and pace of the council's plan to close this gap.
findings.figures: Structural budget gap (STR-01) scored 5×5 = 25 (critical); both 2025/26 and 2026/27 favorable positions attributed to non-recurring sources
findings.quote: While the 2025/26 draft outturn is an improved position, this has been achieved as a result of a number of non-recurring factors which has allowed the Council to take a planned, multi-year approach to strengthen financial resilience, rather than assume sustained improvement in the underlying position. The structural budget gap remains.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership Annual Performance Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Adult protection referrals remain very high at 1,830 per year (153 per month), with increasing complexity and workforce capacity identified as ongoing challenges.
findings.detail: Adult protection is managed through a single point of contact. The volume (1,830 annual referrals, averaging 153 per month) is substantial. The paper notes that 'increasing complexity and ensuring consistency of practice across a large and geographically diverse area, alongside maintaining workforce capacity, remains an ongoing challenge'. This suggests the service may be under strain and unable to fully resource all referrals consistently.
findings.matters: High and acknowledged adult protection demand with known capacity constraints creates governance and safeguarding risk. If the partnership cannot adequately staff this function, there is potential for harm and liability.
findings.figures: 1,830 adult protection referrals in 2025–2026; averaging around 153 referrals per month
findings.quote: during 2025–2026 the service recorded 1,830 adult protection referrals, averaging around 153 referrals per month, highlighting the scale of concerns being identified and managed through the single point of contact for adult protection. Increasing complexity and ensuring consistency of practice across a large and geographically diverse area, alongside maintaining workforce capacity, remains an ongoing challenge.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership Annual Performance Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Mental health crisis demand surged 64% in one year, with 480 people accessing the Distress Brief Intervention service between April 2025 and March 2026.
findings.detail: The Distress Brief Intervention (DBI) service, which provides crisis support at Level 1 and 2, saw demand rise 64% year-on-year. The partnership is responding by recruiting additional staffing (1 WTE Mental Health and Wellbeing Peer Practitioner). This reflects either genuine increase in need or improved access to services. Either way, it signals unmet demand and ongoing resource pressure. The paper does not quantify how much of the savings programme was drawn from mental health.
findings.matters: A 64% surge in crisis mental health demand in one year is material. If the partnership cannot fund expansion, either quality falls or waiting times rise. Mental health underfunding carries both budget and safeguarding risk.
findings.figures: 64% increase between 2024/25 and 2025/26; 480 people accessed support; recruitment of 1 WTE peer practitioner planned
findings.quote: Demand for the service increased by 64% between 2024/25 and 2025/26, with 480 people accessing support between April 2025 and March 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership Annual Performance Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Delayed discharge from hospital deteriorated sharply in 2025/26, rising to 818 days per 1,000 population from 687 in the prior year—a 19% increase in one year.
findings.detail: NI-19 shows a marked deterioration in hospital readiness for discharge over one year (687 to 818 per 1,000 population). This is typically a sign of social care capacity constraints or delayed access to community-based alternatives. The partnership still performs better than Scotland overall (873), but the trend is adverse. Delayed discharge affects both budget (continuing hospital costs) and outcomes (patients stranded in acute beds).
findings.matters: Rising delayed discharge often signals bottleneck in community or social care, a forerunner of demand exceeding capacity. If the trend continues, it may force either emergency spending or admission controls.
findings.figures: NI-19: 818 per 1,000 population in 2025/26; 687 in 2024/25; Scotland average 873
findings.quote: Number of days people aged 75+ spend in hospital when they are ready to be discharged (per 1,000 population): 687 2024/25, 818 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership Annual Performance Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: User-reported experience of health and social care has deteriorated sharply on key outcomes, with five National Indicators now performing more than 5% below the Scottish average.
findings.detail: Aberdeenshire's performance declined between 2023/24 and 2025/26 on the ability to live independently (67.8% vs Scotland 73.6%), having a say in care (55.9% vs 63.9%), service coordination (52.4% vs 65.0%), GP experience (62.2% vs 70.7%), and feeling safe (69.4% vs 74.7%). All five are rated RED. This decline coincides with the budget pressures and service changes implemented during the sustainability programme. The paper acknowledges 'service changes' were made to 'deliver required financial stability' but does not quantify their impact on quality.
findings.matters: Sustained decline in user experience on multiple indicators suggests either the savings programme has hit quality, or demand has outpaced capacity. Either signals operational stress and potential governance risk if service safety is being compromised to meet budget targets.
findings.quote: The data however show a decline in the AHSCP's performance between 2023/24 and 2025/26 in relation to the following indicators, where our current position is now worse than the Scottish position by more than 5%

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership Annual Performance Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: The partnership delivered £19 million of savings in 2025/26, with 70% recurring, achieving a stabilized in-year position after years of deficit.
findings.detail: This is a material positive. The partnership stabilized its financial position through 'strengthened financial management, delivery of planned savings and a continued focus on prioritisation'. The in-year position shifted from chronic overspend to break-even, supported by a significant savings and transformation programme. However, the sustainability of these savings depends on whether they came from service redesign (sustainable) or one-off reductions (temporary).
findings.matters: A council that can deliver recurring savings shows financial discipline and planning capability, reducing refinancing risk. The mix of immediate actions and longer-term redesign matters to debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: £19 million savings; approximately 70% recurring; total budget £485 million
findings.quote: Despite this constrained financial environment, the IJB delivered £19 million of savings during 2025/26, around 70% of which are recurring.

findings.headline: The Council expects to require external borrowing by year-end as internal resources deplete, during a period when interest rates are expected to remain elevated
findings.detail: The Council has undertaken no new long-term external borrowing in the current year, choosing to manage cash balances using internal resources instead. This approach is temporary: the paper states that replacement borrowing will be required as internal resources reduce. This refinancing need will arise in a market environment where 'market expectations have shifted away from further near-term rate reductions towards a more prolonged period of higher rates.'
findings.matters: Understanding when councils must refinance and what rate environment they'll face is critical for assessing future financing costs and financial sustainability
findings.figures: No new long-term borrowing in financial year to date; Investment income £522K to end June 2026
findings.quote: As internal resources reduce later in the year, replacement borrowing may be required through either temporary borrowing or long-term borrowing, depending on market conditions, liquidity requirements and the Council's approved strategy.

findings.headline: Three LOBO loans totalling £30.5m were called with proposed rates 2-3 percentage points higher than existing rates; Council chose to repay at par
findings.detail: DCL Paris loans of £10.0m and £5.5m, and an FMSWM loan of £15.0m, were called with proposed new rates of 6.70%, 6.72%, and 7.48% respectively, compared to existing rates of 3.70%, 4.40%, and 4.65%. The Council exercised its repayment option to avoid accepting these higher rates. The decision avoided further obligation to the higher rates and created no breakage costs, but generates a £30.5m refinancing requirement.
findings.matters: A lender needs to track when councils face material refinancing events and how those are managed; this shows Aberdeenshire had a substantial short-term funding requirement and sufficient liquidity to execute the optimal decision
findings.figures: £10.0m at 3.70% (proposed 6.70%); £5.5m at 4.40% (proposed 6.72%); £15.0m at 4.65% (proposed 7.48%); total £30.5m
findings.quote: The lender option exercises resulted in proposed revised rates that were significantly above the existing loan rates. The Council therefore exercised its option to repay the loans without breakage cost.

findings.headline: Repayment of three market loans requires ongoing monitoring of future refinancing needs
findings.detail: Council has repaid three market loans ahead of maturity, avoiding exposure to higher revised rates. However, this creates a refinancing event and future borrowing requirement that must be monitored in the uncertain interest rate environment. Treasury notes no new long-term borrowing undertaken yet, relying instead on temporary internal borrowing.
findings.matters: Lender needs visibility of council's refinancing schedule and what rates they will face when loans mature; temporary internal borrowing is not a long-term solution
findings.figures: 3 market loans repaid; no new long-term borrowing undertaken
findings.quote: The repayment of three market loans avoided exposure to significantly higher revised rates, although this will require ongoing monitoring of future refinancing requirements.

findings.headline: Council emphasises reserves are finite; cannot provide recurring funding for structural deficit
findings.detail: While current drawdowns are limited and within reserve purpose, council explicitly states reserves cannot solve structural challenges: "Reliance on reserves do not remove the need to identify and deliver recurring savings and sustainable budget solutions." This signals reserves are a depleting asset.
findings.matters: Confirms council cannot rely on reserves to bridge structural gap; future depends on delivering recurring savings or service contraction
findings.figures: (specific reserve balances not provided in main report)
findings.quote: Reserves are a finite resource and can only provide temporary support. The Council continues to face significant medium-term financial challenges and reliance on reserves do not remove the need to identify and deliver recurring savings and sustainable budget solutions.

findings.headline: Two high-rated tactical budget risks (residual score 12) identified but not detailed in main report
findings.detail: The Directorate Risk Register contains two tactical risks with residual score of 12, flagged as requiring continued strategic visibility and active management. The document warns that materialisation "could impact on the overall financial position," but specifics are contained in Appendix 2 and not detailed in the main report.
findings.matters: Known material risks indicate expected pressures; lender needs visibility of what they are and recovery plans if they crystallise
findings.figures: 2 tactical risks, residual score 12
findings.quote: There are currently 2 tactical risks with an updated residual score of 12 indicating the need for continued strategic visibility and these are being actively managed by the Directorate Management Team. Should these risks materialise, this could impact on the overall financial position.

findings.headline: Over half of agreed savings (54%) not yet delivered; delivery remains dependent on future action
findings.detail: Of £0.479m savings agreed at budget setting, only £0.220m (46%) has been achieved by 30 June. A further £0.259m (54%) is assessed as "on track" but unproven. The council notes that "No savings are currently reported as delayed or undeliverable, although delivery remains dependent on completion of the actions set out in Appendix 1."
findings.matters: Unproven savings execution is a material risk; reliance on future delivery creates uncertainty about whether structural challenge can be resolved
findings.figures: £0.220m achieved of £0.479m target; £0.259m (54%) outstanding
findings.quote: Of the £0.479m savings agreed at budget setting, £0.220m has been achieved and £0.259m remains assessed as on track.

findings.headline: Council faces significant medium-term structural budget challenge; current £1.865m underspend is temporary and will unwind
findings.detail: The council is forecasting expenditure £1.865m below its £58.662m revised budget. However, it explicitly warns this is not recurring: the underspend comes from staff vacancies (which will be filled), property income (uncertain to recur), and business rates (due to Inverurie property vacancies). Management states the fundamental structural budget deficit remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Apparent financial health masks ongoing structural deficit; cash position will deteriorate when temporary factors reverse unless recurring savings are delivered
findings.figures: £1.865m underspend on £58.662m budget; £0.259m (54%) of agreed savings still undelivered
findings.quote: The Council continues to face a significant medium-term structural budget challenge. Temporary in-year underspends do not remove the requirement to deliver recurring savings or to ensure that service budgets remain sustainable once vacancies are filled and temporary income or timing effects unwind.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Business Services Budget Risk Register 202627 v2
findings.headline: Licensing fees and charges are underperforming within the income budget
findings.detail: The council has identified pressure within Licensing fees and charges reducing income below forecast. This pressure is currently offset by underspends elsewhere in the Business Services budget, but it represents a loss of income resilience and a specific collection weakness.
findings.matters: Income shortfalls, even when offset, indicate where collection assumptions may be optimistic and reduce the flexibility available to absorb other pressures.
findings.figures: Council Tax collection rates remain strong overall; licensing revenue pressure is isolated to fees and charges within Business Services
findings.quote: Pressure has been identified within Licensing fees and charges however this is currently being offset with underspends across the wider Business Services budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Business Services Budget Risk Register 202627 v2
findings.headline: Repair liabilities on leased properties are under assessment with potential to exceed budgets materially, with a report due to Committee
findings.detail: The council manages leased-out non-income-generating buildings in poor condition requiring landlord repairs and maintenance. An assessment of each repair requirement is currently underway and a report will be brought to Business Services Committee for consideration. The escalation threshold is £1 million; this risk is scored at 4/4 likelihood and impact.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted repair costs on leased assets would create immediate pressure on the capital plan and reduce the council's ability to deliver the property rationalisation programme, directly affecting financial resilience.
findings.figures: Escalation threshold £1 million; risk score 16 (4 likelihood × 4 impact); unchanged from previous period
findings.quote: The Service is currently assessing each repair requirement on an individual basis. A report will be brought to Business Services Committee for consideration once the work has been completed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Council Tax Empty Properties and Second Homes Policy
findings.headline: Council increased Council Tax charges to 300% for long-term empty properties and second homes as part of 2026 budget-setting
findings.detail: Aberdeenshire agreed during budget-setting to raise the premium on long-term empty properties (empty over 12 months) and second homes to 200% above standard Council Tax, creating a 300% total charge from 1 September 2026. This represents an increase from the previous 200% total charge. The policy provides limited deferrals: up to 24 months for empty properties with evidence of active remediation or marketing, and up to 12 months for inherited second homes or exceptional circumstances.
findings.matters: Revenue-raising measures embedded in budget decisions signal how the council is funding its operations. A 50% increase in Council Tax on these property classes is material and suggests the council factored this into its financial planning for 2026–27.
findings.figures: 300% total Council Tax charge (200% premium plus 100% standard charge) effective 1 September 2026; previously 200% total
findings.quote: As part of the 2026 budget-setting decision, the Council agreed to increase the premium to 200% in addition to the standard Council Tax charge from 1 September 2026, meaning a total 300% Council Tax charge will be levied.

findings.headline: Significant savings targets remain undelivered nine months into the financial year
findings.detail: Of £479k in savings identified for 2026/27, only £220k have been achieved to date (46%). Three specific savings are only partially delivered: Woodhill floor-space rental (£0 of £120k), Oxygen Finance rebate (£6k of £40k), and cleaning regime changes (£49k of £154k). All are marked Green as on track, but the execution lag creates material risk to the full-year forecast.
findings.matters: Savings that fall short of target by year-end require offsetting cuts or reserve draws. A lender tracking budget discipline and forward delivery would need to see these high-value targets actually materialise, not remain aspirational.

findings.headline: Licensing fee income increase is not materialising and creates a £100k forecast pressure
findings.detail: The council budgeted for increased licensing fee income as part of 2026/27, but income to date suggests this additional revenue will not be achieved. The paper explicitly flags this as medium residual risk. The council is planning to offset any pressure by identifying corresponding underspends if income remains low.
findings.matters: Income targets that do not materialise directly affect a council's financial resilience and require offsetting spending cuts or reserve draws. A lender tracking budget execution would track whether assumed income gains hold or fall short.
findings.figures: £100k forecast variance; income shortfall flagged as medium residual risk
findings.quote: Income – fees were increased as part of the 2026/27 budget. Income to date would suggest the additional income is not being achieved – forecast is cautious at this early stage in the year.

findings.headline: Staff capacity diverted to Museum of Aberdeenshire capital project is slowing resolution of audit findings
findings.detail: The service attributes slow progress addressing audit issues to competing priorities and staff resourcing constraints while resources are committed to the Museum of Aberdeenshire capital project (scheduled to open 2028). As of audit in March 2026, three loans were due to expire in May 2026 but lenders had not been contacted as required by policy.
findings.matters: Staff capacity constraints around a major capital project may indicate competing demand on management bandwidth, potentially affecting both project delivery and control framework oversight.
findings.figures: Service staffing 9.5 FTE (one seasonal, one project lead for Local Regeneration Fund), Museum of Aberdeenshire project scheduled 2028
findings.quote: Staff are reporting that progress has been slow addressing these issues due to competing priorities

findings.headline: 70% of loans out have expired agreements; 92% lack insurance documentation; 84% lack annual condition reports
findings.detail: Audit testing of 13 loans out found: 9 (70%) have expired agreements, 12 (92%) lack required insurance documentation, and 11 (84%) lack annual condition reports and site visits. Two loans were approved by staff without delegated authority. Items loaned to external venues have not been maintained on loan lists since 2021 and lack insurance coverage.
findings.matters: Uninsured loaned items and expired agreements create unmitigated financial and cultural loss risk; control failures mean items may be damaged, lost, or stolen with no recovery mechanism.
findings.figures: 9 of 13 loans out expired (70%), 12 of 13 lack insurance (92%), 11 of 13 lack condition reports (84%)
findings.quote: Nine (70%) of 13 loan agreements had expired; 12 (92%) lacked insurance documentation; and 11 (84%) lacked annual condition reports and a site visit.

findings.headline: Accreditation expires 31 August 2026 with re-submission due September 2026, while audit identified multiple gaps in required governance policies
findings.detail: The museums face immediate re-accreditation submission deadline. Audit found key required documents are either outdated, missing, or not formally approved, including the Forward Plan, Collections Care and Conservation Policy, Documentation Plan, and Access Plan. These gaps must be resolved within weeks to maintain accreditation status.
findings.matters: Loss of accreditation would damage council reputation, impact grant funding eligibility, and signal inability to meet professional standards; the tight timeline creates execution risk.
